# Histograms {#ggplot2-histogram}

## Introduction

:::{.callout-note}
## Why this chart

Histograms show the shape of one continuous variable: center, spread, skew and gaps.
:::

:::{.callout-warning}
## Common pitfall

Bin width drives the story; try several widths before concluding a distribution is bimodal.
:::

In this chapter, we will learn to

- build histogram
- specify bins
- modify 
    - color
    - fill
    - alpha
    - bin width
    - line type
    - line size
- map aesthetics to variables

A histogram examines the shape and spread of continuous data. It looks very
similar to a bar graph and can be used to detect outliers and skewness in data.
A histogram graphically shows the following:

- center (location) of the data
- spread (dispersion) of the data
- skewness
- outliers
- presence of multiple modes

To construct a histogram, we split the data into intervals called bins. The
intervals may or may not be of equal size. For each bin, we count the number of
data points that fall into it (frequency). The Y axis of the histogram
represents the frequency and the X axis represents the variable.

```{r hist, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE, results='hide', message=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(readr)
```

## Data 

```{r importh, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE}
ecom <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rsquaredacademy/datasets/master/web.csv')
ecom
```

### Data Dictionary

- id: row id
- referrer: referrer website/search engine
- device: device used to visit the website
- bouncers: whether the visit bounced (single page viewed)
- n_visit: number of visits
- n_pages: number of pages visited
- duration: time spent on the website (in seconds)
- country: country of origin
- purchase: whether visitor purchased
- order_items: number of items ordered
- order_value: order value of visitor (in dollars)

## Plot

To create a histogram, we will use `geom_histogram()` and specify the variable
name within `aes()`. In the example below, we create a histogram of the variable
`n_visit`.

```{r hist2, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(ecom) +
  geom_histogram(aes(n_visit))
```

### Specify Bins

The default number of bins in ggplot2 is `30`. You can modify the number of
bins using the `bins` argument. In the example below, we create a histogram
with 7 bins.

```{r hist4, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(ecom) +
  geom_histogram(aes(n_visit), bins = 7)
```

## Aesthetics

Now that we know how to create a histogram, let us learn to modify its 
appearance. We will begin with the background color. Use the `fill` argument
to modify the background color of the histogram. In the example below, we change
the color of the histogram to 'blue'.

```{r hist3, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(ecom) +
  geom_histogram(aes(n_visit), bins = 7, fill = 'blue')
```

As we have learned before, we can modify the transparency of the background
color using the `alpha` argument. It takes any value between `0` and `1`.

```{r hist11, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(ecom) +
  geom_histogram(aes(n_visit), bins = 7, fill = 'blue', alpha = 0.3)
```

We can modify the color of the histogram border using the `color` argument.
Specify the color using its name or the associated hex code.

```{r hist8, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(ecom) +
  geom_histogram(aes(n_visit), bins = 7, fill = 'white', color = 'blue')
```

## Putting it all together

Let us modify the bins, and the background and border color of the histogram in
the example below.

```{r hist9, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(ecom) +
  geom_histogram(aes(n_visit), bins = 7, fill = 'blue', color = 'white')
```

## Bin Width

Another way to control the number of bins in a histogram is to use the
`binwidth` argument. In this case, we specify the width of the bins instead
of their number. In the example below, we do not use the `bins` argument when
using `binwidth`. You can use either of them but not both.

```{r hist5, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(ecom) +
  geom_histogram(aes(n_visit), binwidth = 2, fill = 'blue', color = 'black')
```

## Line Type

We can modify the line type of the histogram border using the `linetype` 
argument. It takes any integer value between `0` and `6`.

```{r hist6, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(ecom) +
  geom_histogram(aes(n_visit), bins = 5, fill = 'white', 
    color = 'blue', linetype = 3)
```

## Line Size

Use the `linewidth` argument to modify the width of the border of the histogram bins.
It takes any value greater than `0`.

```{r hist10, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(ecom) +
  geom_histogram(aes(n_visit), bins = 5, fill = 'white', 
    color = 'blue', linewidth = 1.25)
```

## Map Variables

You can also map the aesthetics to variables. In the example below, we map
`fill` to the device variable. You can try mapping color, linetype and linewidth to
variables too.

```{r hist7, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(ecom) +
  geom_histogram(aes(n_visit, fill = device), bins = 7)
```

## Exercises

1. Draw the `mpg` distribution from `mtcars` with 10 bins.
2. Map density instead of counts using `after_stat()`.
3. Rewrite the plot with a message-first title and labeled axes.
